paragraphs: What happened next was completely unexpected, and it astonished Mitya. A minute earlier he could never have pictured anyone treating him, Mitya Karamazov, this way. Worst of all, it was humiliating, and the other side seemed “supercilious and scornful” about it. Taking off his coat was nothing. But then he was told to strip further. Not asked, really, but “commanded”; he understood that perfectly. Out of pride and contempt he did it without a word. Some peasants had come in with the lawyers and stood on the same side of the curtain. “They’re here in case they need force,” thought Mitya, “and maybe for some other reason, too.”

“Well, do I have to take off my shirt, too?” he asked sharply. Nikolay Parfenovitch didn’t answer. He and the prosecutor were absorbed in going over the coat, the trousers, the waistcoat and the cap, and plainly both of them found it fascinating. “They make no bones about it,” thought Mitya. “They don’t even bother with the most basic politeness.”
“That’s the second time I’ve asked—do I need to take off my shirt or not?” he said, sharper and more irritable still.
“Don’t worry about it. We’ll tell you what to do,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch. His tone was downright domineering, or so Mitya thought.

Meanwhile the lawyers were conferring in low voices. The coat turned out to have a huge patch of blood on it, especially on the left side at the back, dried but still stiff. The trousers had bloodstains, too. On top of that, Nikolay Parfenovitch, with the peasant witnesses looking on, ran his fingers along the collar, the cuffs and every seam of the coat and trousers. He was clearly searching for something—money, of course. He didn’t even hide from Mitya that he suspected him of being able to sew money into his clothes.

“He treats me like a thief, not like an officer,” Mitya muttered to himself. The two of them traded thoughts with amazing openness. The secretary, for example, who was also behind the curtain, bustling around and listening in, pointed out the cap to Nikolay Parfenovitch, which they were also feeling over.

“Remember Gridyenko, the copying-clerk,” said the secretary. “Last summer he got the pay for the whole office, then claimed he’d lost it while drunk. And where did they find it? In piping just like this on his cap. The hundred-rouble notes were rolled up tight and sewn inside the piping.”
Both lawyers remembered Gridyenko’s case very well. They put Mitya’s cap aside and decided that all his clothes would need a closer inspection later.
“Wait,” Nikolay Parfenovitch cried suddenly. He had noticed that the right cuff of Mitya’s shirt was folded under and bloody. “Wait, what’s this—blood?”
“Yes,” Mitya snapped.
“Meaning what blood? ... And why is the cuff folded under?”
Mitya explained that he had got the sleeve bloody tending to Grigory, and had folded it under while washing his hands at Perhotin’s.
“You’ll have to take your shirt off, too. It’s very important as material evidence.”
Mitya went red and exploded with rage.
“What, am I to stay naked?” he shouted.
“Don’t get excited. We’ll sort something out. For now, take off your socks.”
“You’re joking, aren’t you? Is that really necessary?” Mitya’s eyes blazed.
“We’re not in the mood for jokes,” Nikolay Parfenovitch answered sternly.

“Well, if I must—” Mitya muttered. He sat down on the bed and took off his socks. He felt unbearably awkward. Everyone else was dressed and he was naked. Oddly, with his clothes off he somehow felt guilty in front of them. He was nearly ready to believe he really was beneath them, and that they now had every right to look down on him.

“When everybody’s undressed you don’t feel any shame. But when you’re the only one undressed and everyone is staring, it’s degrading,” he kept telling himself over and over. “It’s like a dream. I’ve sometimes dreamed of being in degrading spots like this.” Taking off the socks was torture. They were filthy, and so was his underwear, and now everyone could see. Worse, he disliked his own feet. All his life he had thought both his big toes were hideous. He especially hated the coarse, flat, crooked nail on the right one, and now they’d all see it. The unbearable shame made him deliberately rougher, right away. He yanked off his shirt himself.
“Would you like to search somewhere else, if you’re not too ashamed?”
“No, there’s no need, for now.”
“So am I to stay naked like this?” he added savagely.
“Yes, nothing can be done about that for the moment.... Kindly sit down here a while. You can wrap yourself in a quilt from the bed, and I ... I’ll deal with all this.”

The items were shown to the witnesses. The record of the search was written up. At last Nikolay Parfenovitch left, and the clothes were carried out behind him. Ippolit Kirillovitch left too. That put Mitya alone with the peasants, who stood silent and never took their eyes off him. He wrapped himself in the quilt. He was cold. His bare feet stuck out, and he couldn’t pull the quilt over far enough to cover them. Nikolay Parfenovitch seemed to be gone a long time, “an insufferable time.” “He thinks I’m a puppy,” thought Mitya, grinding his teeth. “And that rotten prosecutor has gone, too. Scorn, no doubt—he can’t stand the sight of me naked!”

Mitya had supposed, though, that they would examine his clothes and hand them back. So he was outraged when Nikolay Parfenovitch returned with entirely different clothes, which a peasant brought in after him.

“Here, clothes for you,” he said airily, looking quite pleased with how his errand had gone. “Mr. Kalganov has kindly supplied these for this unusual emergency, and a clean shirt as well. Fortunately he had them all in his trunk. You can keep your own socks and underwear.”
Mitya blew up.
“I won’t wear other people’s clothes!” he shouted threateningly. “Give me mine!”
“Impossible!”
“Give me mine. And damn Kalganov and his clothes, too!”

It took them a long while to talk him round. But somehow they got him to calm down. They pressed on him that his clothes were stained with blood and so had to be “included with the other material evidence.” They said they “didn’t even have the right to let him keep them now ... given the possible outcome of the case.” At last Mitya understood. He fell into a dark silence and dressed in a hurry. He only observed, as he pulled the things on, that they were a good deal better than his old ones, and that he hated “coming out ahead on the exchange.” And the coat, besides, was “ridiculously tight. Am I to be rigged out like a fool ... for your entertainment?”
They insisted again that he was exaggerating. Kalganov was only slightly taller, they said, so at most the trousers might be a little long. But the coat really was tight across the shoulders.
“Damn it! I can barely do it up,” Mitya grumbled. “Be so kind as to tell Mr. Kalganov from me that I never asked for his clothes, and it’s not my idea that I’ve been dressed up like a clown.”
“He knows that, and he’s sorry ... I mean he’s not sorry to lend you the clothes, he’s sorry about this whole business,” Nikolay Parfenovitch mumbled.
“Confound his sorrow! Well, where to now? Do I just go on sitting here?”

They asked him to go back to the “other room.” Mitya walked in scowling with rage, trying not to meet anyone’s eye. In another man’s clothes he felt disgraced, even in front of the peasants, and Trifon Borissovitch, whose face showed up in the doorway for some reason and vanished at once. “He’s come to see me in my costume,” thought Mitya. He sat down on the same chair as before. He had a ridiculous, nightmarish sense of having lost his mind.

“Well, what next? Are you going to flog me? That’s the only thing you haven’t done,” he said through clenched teeth, speaking to the prosecutor. He refused to turn to Nikolay Parfenovitch, as if he were too proud to speak to him.
“He studied my socks far too closely, and he turned them inside out on purpose, so everyone could see how dirty they were—the scoundrel!”
“Well, now we have to move on to questioning the witnesses,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch, as if in answer to Mitya’s question.
“Yes,” said the prosecutor thoughtfully, as though he were pondering something.

“We’ve done everything we could to help you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Nikolay Parfenovitch continued. “But since you have given us such a flat refusal to say where the money found on you came from, we now find ourselves—”
“What kind of stone is in your ring?” Mitya broke in suddenly, as if waking from a daydream. He pointed at one of the three big rings on Nikolay Parfenovitch’s right hand.
“My ring?” said Nikolay Parfenovitch, surprised.
“Yes, that one ... on your middle finger, with the little veins in it. What stone is it?” Mitya insisted, like a fretful child.
“A smoky topaz,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch, smiling. “Would you like to see it? I’ll take it off ...”

“No, don’t take it off,” Mitya cried furiously, suddenly coming to and angry at himself. “Don’t take it off ... there’s no need.... Damn it!... Gentlemen, you’ve fouled my heart! Do you think I’d hide it from you if I had really killed my father? That I’d wriggle and lie and cover my tracks? No, that’s not Dmitri Karamazov. He couldn’t do it. And if I were guilty, I swear I wouldn’t have sat waiting for you to come, or for sunrise as I first planned. I’d have killed myself before now, without waiting for dawn! I know that about myself now. I couldn’t have learned so much in twenty years as I’ve found out in this accursed night!... And would I be like this tonight, at this moment, sitting with you? Could I talk like this, could I move like this, could I look at you and at the world like this, if I really had murdered my father? When the mere thought that I might have killed Grigory by accident gave me no peace all night—and not from fear—oh, not just from fear of your punishment! The shame of it! And you expect me to be open with scoffers like you, who see nothing and believe in nothing, blind moles and scoffers, and to confess one more nasty thing I’ve done, one more disgrace, even if it would clear me of your accusation! No, Siberia is better! The man who opened the door to my father and walked through it, he killed him, he robbed him. Who was he? I’m racking my brains and I can’t think who. But I can tell you it was not Dmitri Karamazov, and that’s all I can tell you, and that’s enough, enough, leave me alone.... Exile me, punish me, but stop pestering me. I won’t say another word. Call your witnesses!”

Mitya delivered this sudden outburst as if he had resolved to stay completely silent from then on. The prosecutor had watched him throughout. Only when Mitya stopped did he speak, as if it were the most ordinary matter, in a perfectly cold and composed manner:

“Ah, about the open door you mentioned a moment ago. We may as well tell you now, in passing, about a most interesting piece of testimony, extremely important to you and to us alike, which Grigory has given us—the old man you wounded. When he recovered, he stated clearly and emphatically, in answer to our questions, that this is what happened. He came out onto the steps, heard a noise in the garden, and decided to go in by the little gate, which was standing open. Before he saw you running through the dark from the open window where you had seen your father, as you have already told us, Grigory glanced to his left. He noticed the open window, and at the same moment he saw, much closer to him, the door standing wide open—the door you have stated was shut the whole time you were in the garden. I won’t hide from you that Grigory himself firmly affirms and testifies that you must have run out of that door. Naturally he didn’t see you do it with his own eyes, since he first noticed you some distance off in the garden, running toward the fence.”
Mitya had jumped up from his chair halfway through this speech.
“Nonsense!” he yelled in a sudden frenzy. “It’s a barefaced lie. He can’t have seen the door open, because it was shut. He’s lying!”
“It is my duty to repeat that he stands firmly by his statement. He doesn’t waver. He holds to it. We have questioned him closely several times.”
“Exactly. I questioned him several times myself,” Nikolay Parfenovitch confirmed warmly.

“It’s false, false! Either somebody wants to slander me, or it’s a madman’s hallucination,” Mitya kept shouting. “He’s simply raving from loss of blood, from the wound. He must have imagined it when he came to.... He’s raving.”
“Yes, but he noticed the open door not when he came to after being injured, but earlier, as soon as he went into the garden from the lodge.”
“But it’s false, it’s false! It can’t be! He’s slandering me out of spite.... He can’t have seen it ... I didn’t come out of that door,” Mitya gasped.
The prosecutor turned to Nikolay Parfenovitch and told him with emphasis:
“Confront him with it.”
“Do you recognize this object?”
Nikolay Parfenovitch put a large, thick official envelope on the table. Three seals were still unbroken on it. The envelope was empty and torn open at one end. Mitya stared at it, wide-eyed.

“It ... it must be my father’s envelope, the one with the three thousand roubles in it ... and if it’s written on it, let me see, ‘For my little chicken’ ... yes—three thousand!” he shouted. “Do you see, three thousand, do you see?”
“Naturally we see. But the money wasn’t in it. The envelope was empty, on the floor by the bed, behind the screen.”
For a few seconds Mitya stood there as if struck by lightning.
“Gentlemen, it’s Smerdyakov!” he suddenly shouted at the top of his lungs. “He murdered him! He robbed him! Nobody else knew where the old man hid the envelope. It’s Smerdyakov, that’s obvious now!”
“But you also knew about the envelope, and that it was under the pillow.”

“I never knew it. I never saw it. This is the first time I’ve looked at it. I’d only heard about it from Smerdyakov.... He was the only one who knew where the old man kept it hidden; I didn’t know ...” Mitya was completely out of breath.
“But you told us yourself that the envelope was under your late father’s pillow. You specifically said it was under the pillow, so you must have known.”
“It’s written down,” Nikolay Parfenovitch confirmed.

“Nonsense! It’s absurd! I had no idea it was under the pillow. Maybe it wasn’t under the pillow at all.... I just happened to guess it was under the pillow. What does Smerdyakov say? Did you ask him where it was? What does Smerdyakov say? That’s the main point.... And I went out of my way to lie against myself.... I said it was under the pillow without thinking, and now you— Oh, you know how a man says the wrong thing without meaning to. Nobody knew except Smerdyakov, only Smerdyakov, no one else.... He didn’t even tell me where it was! But it’s his doing, his doing; there’s no doubt about it. He murdered him, and that’s as plain as day now,” Mitya cried, more and more wildly, repeating himself without sense, more and more exasperated and worked up. “You must understand that, and arrest him at once.... He must have killed him while I was running away and Grigory was lying unconscious, that’s clear now.... He gave the signal and father opened up to him ... because nobody but he knew the signal, and without the signal father would never have opened the door....”

“But once again you’re overlooking something,” the prosecutor remarked, in the same restrained tone, though with a hint of triumph. “There was no need to give the signal if the door was already standing open when you were there, while you were in the garden....”
“The door, the door,” Mitya muttered, staring at the prosecutor, unable to speak. He sank back in his chair, helpless. Nobody said anything.
“Yes, the door!... It’s a nightmare! God is against me!” he cried, staring straight ahead, utterly stunned.

“Well, you see,” the prosecutor went on with dignity, “you can judge for yourself, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. On one side we have the testimony about the open door you ran out through, a fact that overwhelms you and us alike. On the other side there is your incomprehensible, stubborn and, so to speak, obstinate silence about where the money came from that suddenly appeared in your hands, when only three hours earlier, by your own account, you pawned your pistols for ten roubles! Given all these facts, judge for yourself. What are we to believe, and what can we rely on? And don’t charge us with being ‘frigid, cynical, scoffing people’ who can’t believe in the generous impulses of your heart.... Try to put yourself in our position ...”
Mitya was indescribably agitated. He went pale.
“All right!” he exclaimed suddenly. “I’ll tell you my secret. I’ll tell you where I got the money!... I’ll expose my shame, so I won’t have to blame myself or you afterward.”

“And believe me, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Nikolay Parfenovitch put in, in a tone of almost touching delight, “every honest and full confession from you now may later carry enormous weight in your favor, and may even, furthermore—”
But the prosecutor gave him a slight nudge under the table, and he stopped himself in time. Mitya, true enough, hadn’t heard him.
